newsitem.title: USA: Personal computer market saw robust Q2 growth.
newsitem.headline: Personal computer market saw robust Q2 growth.

text.p: The worldwide personal computer market had a robust second quarter, with shipments up 16 to 17 percent as Dell Computer Corp's unbridled growth continued and Hewlett-Packard Co. had a surprising surge.
On Monday, two market research firms release second-quarter data, both showing substantial, better-than-expected growth in the United States, driven by corporate sales.

International Data Corp (IDC), of Framingham, Mass., said that by geography, the United States was the strongest, with 19 percent unit growth. Asia/Pacific grew 14 percent while Japan grew only six percent, as economic uncertainty, high prices and a new consumer tax depressed demand. Western Europe had better-than-expected growth of 11 percent.

Both IDC and Dataquest Inc., of San Jose, Calif., said Compaq Computer Corp. remained the world's top PC vendor, followed by No. 2 International Business Machines Corp., with Hewlett-Packard as a surprising No. 3, Dell Computer remaining No. 4 and Packard Bell NEC in fifth place.
The top four PC vendors worldwide -- Compaq, IBM, H-P and Dell -- all had unit growth rates that vastly outpaced the rest of the market, ranging from 20 to 61 percent.

"We have not seen this kind of situation since IBM dominated the industry," said Scott Miller, a Dataquest analyst. "The middle tier players are getting squeezed. It's going to get tougher to compete and there is a possibility we will see some consolidation in this market. We have a real concentration of share going on."
According to Dataquest's preliminary data, PC unit shipments worldwide were up 17 percent, to 18.9 million, from 16.2 million in the second quarter a year ago.

IDC said that units were up 16 percent, to 18.2 million, from 15.9 milion in the second quarter of 1996. IDC said its shipment numbers are branded shipments only and exclude original equipment manufacturer sales for all vendors.

Compaq, the world leader, shipped 2.2 million machines in the second quarter, with unit growth of of 42 percent, Dataquest said. IBM shipped 1.7 million units, for 20 percent growth, the slowest growth rate of the top five.

Hewlett-Packard's units skyrocketed 58.4 percent to 1.04 million, and it jumped to third place among leading vendors from sixth place a year ago. Dell again had the fastest growth in the industry, at 61.4 percent, with 1.01 million units shipped, while Packard Bell NEC's growth dropped 1.7 percent, to 932,000 units.

Other vendors posted 9.7 percent growth for the same period. Apple Computer Inc., for the second quarter in a row, did not make it into the ranking of the top five PC vendors. According to IDC's preliminary data, Apple was either No. 8 or 9, with about 698,000 units in the second quarter.

"They had a tough quarter," said Kevin Hause, an IDC analyst. "Shaken consumer confidence in the brand is continuing to hurt it in retail. Hopefully they will get a new CEO and a new vision and a new approach to the PC market."

Both Dataquest and IDC said the market consolidation has been in part fueled by the major success of Dell, which has lower costs and offers lower prices because of its build-to-order manufacturing strategy and selling directly to the customer, bypassing all distribution channels.
Compaq, H-P and IBM have all been changing their manufacturing and distribution models in order to better compete with Dell and offer lower prices.
"The indirect guys are doing the right stuff and it's starting to show," said Dataquest's Miller. "Part of it is pricing. You are seeing unprecedented competition at the top."
Both firms expect the rest of the year to be strong, with new products in the second half, as the rivalry intensifies.

"Dell's continued operational effectiveness is something you can write case studies about," IDC's Hause said. "They are moving along at a healthy clip and we have the No. 1 vendor in the world openly chasing their model. I don't see anything stopping them soon."
